articles.title: Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram
articles.summary: Meta’s AI assistant can track and unfollow Instagram users who don’t follow you back—and some people are taking full advantage.
body: Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse — Meta ’s AI assistant —could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

“I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old New Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”

Within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”
points: Meta’s AI assistant can track and unfollow Instagram users who don’t follow you back—and some people are taking full advantage.

articles.title: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots
articles.summary: The Jensen Huang scandal is the latest fuel for dating anxieties among newly rich and powerful tech workers.
body: When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson says, because he was “super worried about spies.”

The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may have ulterior motives: accessing corporate secrets.
“Even if you're not a CEO or at a big tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.
One tech worker, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly, says he considers himself “highly selective” about the people he interacts with face-to-face.

articles.title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
articles.summary: Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That's according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic…
body: Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.

An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.

articles.title: This 16-Year-Old Founded an AI Missile Startup. He’s Targeting ‘Cost per Kill’
articles.summary: Henrijs Dandzbergs dropped out of high school to join startup accelerator Y Combinator. With a new breed of missile, he wants to make killing as efficient as possible for the US and its military allies.
body: At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided- missile startup.

In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.

His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”

In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.

articles.title: AI helps researchers investigate how thousands of medical studies share code
articles.summary: An MIT and Dana-Farber Institute-led team used large language models to examine nearly 4,000 studies and hundreds of code repositories, revealing gaps in the information needed to scrutinize and reuse published research.
body: The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated?
Access to a study's data and code help researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods, and to build on the work.

“Studies involve many choices about how to prepare data, develop models, and evaluate performance. These are sometimes called ‘researcher degrees of freedom,’” says Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. “The choices we make affect the results, and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail.”

While sharing code can be a first step, in order for code to be understood and reused, it must be sufficiently structured and described. The problem is that, right now, there is little guidance for researchers on what constitutes a well-organized, well-described collection of code.

articles.title: Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
articles.summary: Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google's vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.
body: You can now view your recent AI searches by opening the sidebar on Google’s homepage.

Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.

It’s yet another big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. The company brought its AI Mode button to its search bar last year, which opens up a chatbot-like search experience within Google. In May, Google updated its search box to accommodate longer queries and added AI-powered autocomplete.

Stein says Google is rolling out the option because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.” The new homepage is rolling out globally on desktop.

articles.title: Study reveals data centers’ long-distance damage to air quality
articles.summary: Researchers find air pollution from data center electricity use can affect communities far from the facilities, with some of the highest impacts in the Midwest.
body: Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license. The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers.
The team estimates that additional air pollution from the electricity demands of data centers in 2023 resulted in about 650 premature deaths across the United States.

Some Midwestern states had among the highest estimated rates of premature deaths per capita attributable to data centers, even though much of the data center electricity demand was concentrated in Virginia and Texas.

articles.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
articles.summary: Are the recent outages in the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms really a coincidence? There's actually likely something deeper going on, cybersecurity experts say.
body: It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.

Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.

The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.

body: Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”
The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”

articles.title: This featherweight, flying robot carries its own sensors and computers
articles.summary: The speedy microrobot flies without an attached motion-capture system, moving it closer to applications like agriculture or industrial surveillance.
body: Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license. You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided below, credit the images to "MIT."

Over the past decade, MIT researchers have developed aerial microrobots with bumblebee-like speed, agility, and durability, for tasks like precision agriculture or search-and-rescue. But these featherweight microrobots couldn’t carry the electronics needed for navigation, forcing them to remain connected to a motion-capture system in the lab.

Now, the researchers have designed a flapping-wing microrobot with onboard sensors and computation, which can follow a complex trajectory and land precisely on a sunflower outside the lab’s motion capture environment.
While the robot is still connected to an offboard power source, this demonstration highlights the potential of aerial microrobots to be used for precision agriculture in the future.

articles.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
articles.summary: At the upgraded $83/share IPO price, Anthropic's seven founders each pocketed $280 million, while the company nabbed nearly $105 billion.
body: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”
points: At the upgraded $83/share IPO price, Anthropic's seven founders each pocketed $280 million, while the company nabbed nearly $105 billion.

articles.title: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
articles.summary: Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia following an affair, which could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
body: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.

The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
points: Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia following an affair, which could have ramifications for national security as the U.S. and China race to develop the most advanced AI infrastructure.
